report.releaseDate: 1 Oct 2026 (DICJ Sept/9M GGR); 17 Oct 2026 (DICJ Q3 by game); 26 Oct 2026 (DSEC 9M arrivals); 12 Oct 2026 (DSF 9M gaming tax)
report.currency: MOP (Macau pataca) — tables in MOP billions unless stated, with ~USD alongside at USD/MOP 8.07
report.verdict: Macau's 9M-2026 casino GGR of MOP187.12bn (~$23.19bn, +3.2% YoY) flatters a market that has rolled over: four straight monthly year-on-year declines through September (five through October), a Q3 of MOP60.22bn (~$7.46bn, -3.8%) driven by a 7.9% fall in mass/premium-mass baccarat, and GGR per visitor down ~5% even as arrivals rose 8.5%. The regime is stable but closed — six concessions locked to 31 Dec 2032, a 40% effective levy on GGR, zero licensed online — so for B2Tech the only realistic exposure is B2B supply into the one product line still growing, slots (+~19% YoY).
summary: **World's largest casino market, but growth has stalled:** DICJ-reported casino GGR for Jan–Sep 2026 was MOP187.12bn (~$23.19bn), +3.2% YoY; through October it was MOP208.79bn (~$25.87bn), +1.6%. FY2025 was MOP247.40bn (~$30.66bn), +9.1%, still only 84.6% of 2019's MOP292.46bn (~$36.24bn). All figures are gross gaming revenue (win before tax); Macau does not report NGR.

**The trajectory inside the 9M number is negative:** cumulative growth decayed from +24.0% (Jan) to +12.1% (4M), +6.8% (H1), +3.2% (9M) and +1.6% (10M). Quarterly: Q1 +14.5% (MOP66.04bn, ~$8.18bn), Q2 flat (MOP61.2bn, ~$7.58bn), Q3 -3.8% (MOP60.22bn, ~$7.46bn). Monthly YoY: Jun -12.1%, Jul -8.4%, Aug -1.2%, Sep -1.2%, Oct -10.0% — five consecutive declines, October falling despite Golden Week.

**Product mix — it is a premium-mass problem, not a VIP problem:** Q3 mass baccarat (DICJ's line includes premium mass) fell 7.9% to MOP33.61bn (~$4.16bn), a MOP2.88bn (~$357m) decline larger than the whole market's MOP2.35bn (~$291m) fall; VIP baccarat was flat at MOP16.91bn (~$2.10bn, +0.1%); slots +18.8% to MOP4.09bn (~$0.51bn); live multi-game ETGs -8% to ~MOP1.14bn (~$0.14bn). Summing the three DICJ quarterlies: 9M mass baccarat MOP105.4bn (~$13.06bn, ~-1%), VIP MOP52.4bn (~$6.49bn, ~+10%), slots MOP12.2bn (~$1.51bn, ~+19%).

**Baccarat is the market:** baccarat (mass + VIP) was 85.1% of GGR across 16 approved games of fortune in 2025 (DICJ); in Q3-26 mass baccarat was 55.8% of GGR and VIP baccarat 28.0%, so ~84% combined. Slots have only reached 6.8% of GGR (from 5.5% a year earlier) — the single structural growth line.

**Channel: 100% land-based, 0% licensed online.** Law 16/2001 (as revised by Law 7/2022) licenses only casino games of fortune in physical casinos; there is no interactive/online licence class and no proposal to create one. 'Online penetration' is therefore nil by law; any digital exposure is illegal cross-border activity targeted by Macau's 2022 illegal-gambling law and the PRC's criminalisation of cross-border gambling.

**Licensing regime — closed until 2032:** six concessions (SJM Resorts, Galaxy Casino, Venetian Macau/Sands China, Melco Resorts (Macau), Wynn Resorts (Macau), MGM Grand Paradise) awarded 16 Dec 2022 by Executive Orders 218–223/2022 after a 29 Jul–14 Sep 2022 tender with seven bidders; 10-year contracts effective 1 Jan 2023. The revised law caps concessions at six and abolished sub-concessions. No new B2C entry is possible before a re-tender ahead of 31 Dec 2032.

**Consolidation is complete:** 20 casinos now operate (SJM 5, Sands 5, Galaxy 3, Melco 3, Wynn 2, MGM 2) versus a 2021 peak of 42, after the three-year transition for third-party 'satellite' casinos ended 31 Dec 2025 with none surviving; their ~480 tables and ~270 machines (June 2025, DICJ) were reallocated to the concessionaires. The floor stock is ~6,000 tables and ~12,000 machines (DICJ, end-2025 and end-H1 2026).

**Tax regime — base is GGR, headline 35%, effective 40%:** Article 27 of the gaming law levies a 35% special gaming tax on gross gaming revenue, payable by the 10th of the following month, plus mandated contributions of up to 5% of GGR (public foundation, urban development/tourism/social security), giving a 40% effective rate — among the highest GGR-based rates of any major casino jurisdiction. No change was enacted or proposed in 2026. Fixed/variable annual premiums per table and machine and minimum-GGR-per-table top-ups also apply [parameters not re-verified this session].

**Tax take:** DSF recorded MOP74.56bn (~$9.24bn) of gaming revenue in Jan–Sep 2026, +5.9% YoY (Sept alone MOP8.39bn, ~$1.04bn), equal to 80.6% of the FY2026 gaming-tax budget of MOP92.53bn (~$11.47bn) and 84.1% of government current revenue (MOP88.71bn, ~$10.99bn). FY2025 gaming taxes were MOP94.9bn (~$11.76bn), +7.6%, 76.6% of total government revenue of MOP124.1bn (~$15.38bn).

**Government target will be met, but says little:** the 2026 budget assumes GGR of MOP236bn (~$29.24bn), already below 2025's actual MOP247.4bn; 79% was achieved by September, and Nov–Dec need only MOP27.2bn (~$3.37bn) versus MOP41.98bn (~$5.20bn) in Nov–Dec 2025. CE Sam Hou Fai has refused to revise the figure. Our estimate for FY2026 is MOP245–250bn (~$30.4–31.0bn), i.e. -1% to +1% YoY [estimate].

**Visitation is rising while spend per head falls:** DSEC counted 32,181,272 arrivals in 9M-26 (+8.5%); September's 3,216,535 (+15.9%) was driven by same-day visitors (+23.8% to 1.93m) rather than overnight (+5.7% to 1.28m). International arrivals were only 1,949,417 (+3.4%), ~6% of the total. Implied GGR per visitor was ~MOP5,815 (~$721) in 9M-26, ~-4.9% YoY, and ~MOP5,615 (~$696) in September, ~-15% YoY.

**Operator landscape:** six concessionaires; DICJ does not publish operator GGR shares, so market-share data is n/a from primary sources (company filings would be required). Galaxy's Q3 release corroborates the market: HKD181.7bn 9M market GGR (+3%) and HKD58.5bn in Q3 (-4%).

**VIP and junkets — smaller, concessionaire-controlled, and volatile:** DICJ defines VIP by table classification, not by junket play. VIP baccarat jumped +35.4% in Q1 (MOP19.56bn, ~$2.42bn; 29.7% share), fell 18.8% QoQ in Q2 on low hold and the World Cup, and recovered +6.3% QoQ in Q3. Licensed gaming promoters numbered 29 at end-June 2026 (31 at end-March). Seaport estimates October VIP GGR fell >35% YoY, citing mainland capital controls — the segment remains hostage to PRC policy.

**Payments reality:** play is cash/chip-based (HKD-denominated chips dominate), with mainland UnionPay and cross-border cash subject to PRC capital controls; there is no licensed digital-wallet or online funding channel. Capital-control enforcement is a direct GGR driver (Seaport's October VIP read) rather than a compliance footnote.

**Responsible gambling and advertising are restrictive and stable:** minimum entry/employment age is 21 (Law 10/2012), a DICJ-administered self-exclusion scheme exists, main-floor smoking is prohibited with approved lounges, and direct advertising of games of fortune is prohibited in Macau — concessionaires market the resort, not the game [regime details from statute, not re-read this session].

**Enforcement and political direction of travel:** tighter, not looser. The 2022 package (Law 7/2022 gaming law, Law 16/2022 on gaming promoters, the illegal-gambling law) ended junket revenue-share and junket-run VIP rooms, closed satellites, and tied concessions to non-gaming investment pledges; Beijing's criminalisation of cross-border gambling continues. Policy priority is fiscal stability and 'adequate diversification', not market expansion.

**Labour:** 53,272 persons engaged in gaming at end-2025 (10.7% of a 496,600 labour force, DSEC); average full-time gaming earnings MOP28,660 (~$3,551)/month in June 2026 (+4.6%), dealers (41.9% of the workforce) MOP22,130 (~$2,742, +1.5%). Wage inflation against falling GGR compresses operator margins.

**Non-casino betting is immaterial:** Macau Slot's exclusive football and basketball concession generated MOP90m (~$11.2m, -10%) and MOP73m (~$9.0m, +23.7%) respectively in Q1-26 — ~0.25% of casino GGR; the concession was extended to 5 Jun 2026 pending a review of the sports-betting model (outcome after that date: n/a). Horse racing ended 1 Apr 2024; greyhound racing ended 20 Jul 2018.

**Read-through for B2Tech:** there is no B2C route (no licence class, no online, no sub-concessions, next tender 2032). The commercially live exposure is B2B — slot/ETG supply and content into a floor that is shifting premium-mass players onto machines (slots +19%, 12,000 machines, consolidated into six buyers) — or services to concessionaires/promoters, each requiring DICJ approval. Entry economics must assume a 40% GGR levy on the operator side, a demand base that is ~95% Greater China, and policy risk set in Beijing rather than Macau.

**Data caveats:** DICJ's quarterly by-game series sums to MOP187.46bn for 9M-26 versus MOP187.12bn in the monthly series (~0.2% definitional/timing gap); one outlet (GGRAsia) printed September GGR as MOP17.84bn against MOP18.06bn in all other reports — we use MOP18.06bn, consistent with October's reported +20.0% MoM.

segments.name: Market trajectory & demand (monthly GGR, visitation)
segments.headline: A +3.2% nine-month print built entirely on Q1; the run-rate since June is negative and October's -10% came in a Golden Week month.
narrative: The 2026 monthly series tells a cleaner story than the cumulative figure. January opened at MOP22.63bn (~$2.80bn, +24.0%), March matched it at MOP22.61bn (~$2.80bn, +15.0%), and May repeated MOP22.61bn (+6.7%) — three of the strongest post-pandemic months. From June the comparison base (2025's own recovery) stiffened and demand softened: June MOP18.52bn (~$2.29bn, -12.1%), July MOP20.26bn (~$2.51bn, -8.4%), August MOP21.89bn (~$2.71bn, -1.2%), September MOP18.06bn (~$2.24bn, -1.2%, the lowest month since September 2024), and October MOP21.68bn (~$2.69bn, -10.0%) against MOP24.09bn (~$2.99bn) a year earlier. The 9M total of MOP187.12bn (~$23.19bn) is +3.2% only because Q1 was +14.5%.

The World Cup (expanded 48-team, 104-match format, June–July) is the consensus explanation for June and July, and CreditSights argues those months should be excluded when assessing structural health. But August, September and October all declined without a tournament, and October — which contained National Day Golden Week and the NBA China Games at the Venetian — fell by the second-largest margin of the year. The honest reading is that the base effect from 2025's strong second half is now compounded by weaker spend per head, not merely by calendar noise.

Visitation is not the constraint. DSEC recorded 32,181,272 arrivals in 9M-26 (+8.5%) and 3,216,535 in September (+15.9%); Q3 alone brought ~11.2m (+8% YoY, +15% QoQ). The composition is the issue: September's growth came from same-day visitors (+23.8% to 1,933,257) rather than overnight guests (+5.7% to 1,283,278), and international arrivals (1,949,417 in 9M, +3.4%) are only ~6% of the total despite being the stated diversification target of the concession contracts. Dividing DICJ GGR by DSEC arrivals gives ~MOP5,815 (~$721) per visitor in 9M-26, about 4.9% below the ~MOP6,113 (~$757) of 9M-25, and ~MOP5,615 (~$696) in September, ~15% below September 2025.

For the FY2026 outcome the arithmetic is settled: 10M GGR of MOP208.79bn (~$25.87bn) leaves only MOP27.2bn (~$3.37bn) needed across November and December to hit the government's MOP236bn (~$29.24bn) budget assumption, against MOP41.98bn (~$5.20bn) delivered in the same two months of 2025. Seaport's November forecast is -6.1% YoY (~MOP19.8bn, ~$2.45bn) with VIP down more than 35% in October. We model FY2026 at MOP245–250bn (~$30.4–31.0bn), -1% to +1% YoY [estimate], meaning the market's first flat-to-down year since reopening, masked by a target set below the prior-year actual.

For an operator the implication is that Macau's volume engine (visitor count) is intact but its value engine (overnight, premium-mass spend from the mainland) is not, and the gap is widening month by month. This is the metric to track rather than headline GGR: the same-day/overnight mix and GGR-per-visitor are the earliest indicators of whether Q4-26 stabilises.

segments.name: Mass market: premium mass, grind mass, slots & ETGs
segments.headline: Mass baccarat — 56% of GGR and the post-junket growth engine — fell 7.9% in Q3; slots are the only line compounding.
narrative: DICJ's quarterly by-game series separates 'baccarat' (mass and premium-mass tables) from 'VIP baccarat' (tables classified as VIP). Mass baccarat produced MOP36.56bn (~$4.53bn, +6.5%) in Q1, MOP35.2bn (~$4.36bn, -1.2%) in Q2 and MOP33.61bn (~$4.16bn, -7.9% YoY, -4.4% QoQ) in Q3, taking its share from 59.4% a year earlier to 55.8%. The Q3 decline of MOP2.88bn (~$357m) exceeded the whole market's MOP2.35bn (~$291m) fall — i.e. every other product combined was positive. Summed over 9M, mass baccarat was ~MOP105.4bn (~$13.06bn), roughly -1% YoY, against +6.5% at the end of Q1.

The broader mass segment including slots and ETGs was MOP45.13bn (~$5.59bn, +0.8%) in Q2 and MOP43.31bn (~$5.37bn, -5.2%, -4.0% QoQ) in Q3, at 71.9% of GGR. Because premium mass is where the concessionaires reinvested after junket VIP was dismantled in 2022–23, this is the segment that determines EBITDA margins and the one most exposed to mainland wealth effects, property-market sentiment and capital-control enforcement. Trade commentary on April already pointed to 'low VIP hold', but no such hold explanation exists for three consecutive quarters of mass-baccarat weakening.

Slot machines are the counter-trend: MOP3.98bn (~$0.49bn, +21.6%) in Q1, MOP4.11bn (~$0.51bn, +17.0%) in Q2 and MOP4.09bn (~$0.51bn, +18.8%) in Q3, lifting the category's share to 6.8% from 5.5%. Live multi-game ETGs were MOP1.26bn (~$0.16bn, +3.5%), MOP1.30bn (~$0.16bn, +3.1%) and ~MOP1.14bn (~$0.14bn, -8%). The drivers are structural rather than cyclical: table counts are administratively capped (~6,000), satellite-casino tables and machines were reallocated to the concessionaires' own floors at end-2025, and operators are steering lower-value mass play to machines. Even so, a 6.8% share means slot growth cannot offset a premium-mass customer who stops coming — a ~MOP0.65bn (~$80m) YoY slot gain versus a MOP2.88bn (~$357m) mass-baccarat loss in Q3.

Floor supply is static at ~6,000 tables and ~12,000 machines (DICJ, end-2025 and end-H1 2026), spread over 20 casinos. With the quarterly mass segment at ~MOP43–45bn, the market is yielding roughly MOP2.4bn (~$0.30bn) of mass GGR per 1,000 tables per quarter, a productivity level that the concessionaires can only lift through premium-mass yield — exactly the variable that is deteriorating.

Commercially, the mass data set two messages for a B2B supplier. First, the addressable spend on machine product and systems is growing double-digit in a market where everything else is flat or down, and consolidation into six buyers simplifies distribution but raises negotiating power on the buyer side. Second, any revenue-share or performance-linked structure should be modelled on mass GGR falling mid-single-digit in H2-26, not on the 9M headline.

segments.name: VIP baccarat & gaming promoters (junkets)
segments.headline: VIP is now a concessionaire-run, ~28%-of-GGR product: +35% in Q1 on hold and base effects, -19% QoQ in Q2, flat YoY in Q3, and reportedly -35% in October.
narrative: DICJ's 'VIP baccarat' is a table classification inside the integrated resorts, not a measure of junket-intermediated play, and the concessionaires' own VIP/premium-direct definitions differ materially. On DICJ's basis VIP baccarat generated MOP19.56bn (~$2.42bn, +35.4% YoY, 29.7% share) in Q1-26, MOP15.90bn (~$1.97bn, -2.6% YoY, -18.8% QoQ, 26.0% share) in Q2 and MOP16.91bn (~$2.10bn, +0.1% YoY, +6.3% QoQ, 28.0% share) in Q3 — ~MOP52.4bn (~$6.49bn) over nine months, roughly +10% YoY on our summation. Q1's surge coincided with entertainment-led premium promotion (concerts, branded events) and a weak Q1-25 base; Q2's drop was attributed by analysts to low hold and the World Cup.

The Q1-to-Q3 share range of 26–30% compares with 30.7% in Q4-25 and ~25% in Q1-25, so the product is oscillating within a band rather than recovering toward the 50–60% it held in the junket era. The structural ceiling is regulatory: Law 16/2022 (effective 1 Jan 2023) limits each gaming promoter to one concessionaire, bans revenue-sharing in favour of commission-only remuneration, prohibits junket-operated VIP rooms and deposit-taking, and makes concessionaires liable for promoter conduct [statute parameters not re-read this session]. The promoter population reflects this: 29 licensed gaming promoters at end-June 2026, down from 31 at end-March, versus well over a hundred before 2022.

Forward indicators are poor. Seaport estimated October VIP GGR fell more than 35% YoY while mass fell low-single-digit, pointing to mainland capital controls, and forecast November market GGR at -6.1%. Because VIP is now mostly premium-direct credit extended by the concessionaires themselves, VIP volatility flows straight to operator receivables and provisions rather than being absorbed by junket balance sheets as it once was.

For B2Tech, the VIP/junket channel is not an entry point: gaming-promoter licences are annual, DICJ-vetted, commission-capped and tied to a single concessionaire, and the economics without revenue share do not support an independent operator model. The relevant read-through is that VIP is a hold-driven, policy-driven swing factor of ±MOP3–4bn (~$0.4–0.5bn) per quarter that makes market GGR forecasting — and any revenue-linked B2B contract — unusually noisy.

segments.name: Licensing & concession regime
segments.headline: Six 10-year concessions to 31 Dec 2032, no sub-concessions, no online class and no satellites: the most closed major casino jurisdiction in the world.
narrative: The enabling statute is Law 16/2001 'Legal Framework for the Operations of Casino Games of Fortune', substantially revised by Law 7/2022 (passed 21 June 2022, gazetted 22 June 2022) with Administrative Regulation 28/2022 governing the tender. The Gaming Inspection and Coordination Bureau (DICJ) regulates and inspects; the Financial Services Bureau (DSF) assesses and collects gaming taxes and may audit concessionaires and promoters jointly with DICJ. The revised law fixes the maximum number of concessions at six, abolishes sub-concessions (the pre-2022 structure had three concessions and three sub-concessions), and caps terms at ten years (extendable by up to three years in exceptional circumstances) [extension clause not re-read this session].

The 2022 tender ran 29 July–14 September 2022 with seven bidders; provisional results were announced 26 November 2022 (Executive Order 205/2022) and definitive awards on 16 December 2022 (Executive Orders 218–223/2022) to MGM Grand Paradise, Galaxy Casino, Venetian Macau, Melco Resorts (Macau), Wynn Resorts (Macau) and SJM Resorts — the six incumbents. Contracts took effect 1 January 2023 and run to 31 December 2032. The seventh bidder (Genting) was unsuccessful, and there has been no public signal of a licence expansion, so the next entry window is the re-tender process ahead of 2033.

Conditions attached to the 2023 concessions are what distinguish this cycle. Concessionaires are Macau-incorporated with a minimum share capital of MOP5bn (~$620m) and a Macau-permanent-resident managing director holding at least 15% of capital [thresholds not re-read this session]; they pledged non-gaming investment across ten categories (MICE, entertainment, sport, culture, health, themed attractions) as part of the DICJ-stated strategy to 'explore overseas customer markets', with DICJ explicitly committing to 'follow up closely on the implementation of the investment projects'. Third-party-operated 'satellite' casinos were given a three-year transition that expired 31 December 2025; none continued, and the 11 venues' ~480 tables and ~270 machines were reallocated to the sponsoring concessionaires rather than reverting to the government. The casino count fell from 42 (2021) to 20.

Economic terms layered on the 35% tax include an annual concession premium (a fixed component of MOP30m (~$3.7m) plus MOP300,000 (~$37k) per VIP table, MOP150,000 (~$19k) per mass table and MOP1,000 (~$124) per machine, subject to a minimum) and a minimum annual GGR per table and per machine below which the shortfall is taxed as if earned [all unverified this session — from the statute as known]. The practical consequence is that table allocations are a managed resource and that marginal, low-yield tables are a cost, reinforcing the shift of grind-mass play to machines.

For an operator weighing Macau the licensing conclusion is binary: there is no B2C path until the early 2030s, and even then the 2022 process showed incumbency, local-resident shareholding, non-gaming pledges and political acceptability outweigh gaming expertise. The realistic routes are gaming-equipment supply (machines and systems certified against DICJ technical standards and supplied through approved manufacturers/distributors), management or technology services contracted to a concessionaire, or a gaming-promoter licence — each DICJ-approved, each dependent on a concessionaire counterparty.

segments.name: Tax & fiscal dependence
segments.headline: A 40% effective levy on GGR delivered MOP74.56bn (~$9.24bn) in nine months — 84% of government current revenue — which is precisely why the regime will not loosen.
narrative: The tax base is gross gaming revenue, not turnover and not net revenue after promotional allowances. Article 27 of the gaming law sets the special gaming tax at 35% of GGR, payable monthly by the 10th; the concession contracts add contributions of up to 2% of GGR to a public foundation and up to 3% to urban development, tourism promotion and social security, for an effective 40% [contribution split per concession contracts; not re-read this session]. There is no player-level withholding on winnings and no corporate-level profits tax on gaming income beyond the special tax (concessionaires have historically been exempted from complementary tax on gaming profits by executive dispensation) [unverified this session]. No change to any of these parameters was enacted or formally proposed in 2026.

DSF's central-account data show gaming receipts of MOP74.56bn (~$9.24bn) for January–September 2026, +5.9% YoY, after MOP34.87bn (~$4.32bn, +16.9%) at 4M, MOP51.19bn (~$6.34bn, +13%) at H1 and MOP66.17bn (~$8.20bn, +6.9%) at 8M. The decay in the growth rate lags GGR by roughly a month because tax is remitted on the prior month's win; September receipts of MOP8.39bn (~$1.04bn) relate largely to August GGR of MOP21.89bn. Receipts equal 39.8% of 9M GGR, consistent with the 40% effective rate once timing is allowed for. Against the FY2026 gaming-tax budget of MOP92.53bn (~$11.47bn), 80.6% was collected in nine months, so the budget will be exceeded even on a weak Q4 — we estimate FY2026 receipts of MOP96–99bn (~$11.9–12.3bn) [estimate].

Dependence is extreme and rising: gaming taxes were 84.1% of government current revenue of MOP88.71bn (~$10.99bn) in 9M-26 (86.4% at 8M, 86.5% at 4M), and in FY2025 gaming concession revenue was 76.6% of total government revenue of MOP124.1bn (~$15.38bn), with gaming taxes of MOP94.9bn (~$11.76bn, +7.6%) exceeding the MOP93.1bn (~$11.54bn) budget. The Legislative Assembly's budget committee (11 November 2026) explicitly recorded that reliance 'remains unchanged'. FY2025 expenditure was MOP102.9bn (~$12.75bn), so the surplus itself depends on the 40% levy.

The policy consequence cuts both ways for a prospective entrant. On one hand the government has no fiscal room to raise the rate without damaging the base, and every signal (target maintenance, refusal to revise forecasts, event subsidies) is about protecting GGR; on the other, this dependence is the reason the 2022 law added minimum-GGR-per-table rules, non-gaming investment pledges and the power to terminate concessions on national-security grounds — the state's leverage over operators is total. An operator model for Macau must assume 40% of GGR plus premium plus mandated reinvestment as the fixed cost of the licence, with no realistic prospect of relief.

segments.name: Payments, AML, responsible gambling & advertising
segments.headline: Cash, chips and UnionPay under PRC capital controls; no legal digital funding rail; a 21+ floor with no gaming advertising — restrictions are stable, but Beijing's enforcement is the swing variable.
narrative: Macau's payment reality is unusual among major gaming markets: there is no licensed online channel, so there is no e-wallet, card-not-present or open-banking funding of play. Casino floors transact in HKD-denominated chips (MOP is pegged to HKD at 1.03, HKD to USD), funded by cash, by mainland UnionPay cards (subject to PRC annual overseas cash-withdrawal caps and transaction monitoring) and by concessionaire-extended credit for premium-direct players [UnionPay limits and the extent of operator credit not re-verified this session]. Seaport's attribution of October's >35% VIP fall to 'China capital controls' illustrates that payment friction set in Beijing is a first-order driver of Macau GGR, not a back-office issue.

AML sits under Macau's AML/CFT law (Law 2/2006) and DICJ instructions on customer due diligence, large-transaction and suspicious-transaction reporting, with the Financial Intelligence Office (GIF) as the FIU [thresholds not re-read this session]. The 2022 gaming law amendments made concessionaires jointly responsible for gaming-promoter conduct, and the 2022 illegal-gambling law criminalised unauthorised gaming, side-betting and the operation of illegal online gambling from Macau; on the mainland, the 2021 amendment to PRC Criminal Law Article 303 criminalised organising cross-border gambling for PRC citizens. The practical effect is that any operator-facing model that touches mainland customer acquisition — including digital marketing — carries criminal, not merely regulatory, risk.

Responsible-gambling rules are codified rather than operator-discretionary: Law 10/2012 sets the entry and employment age at 21 and bars off-duty casino staff from gaming floors; DICJ runs a self-exclusion/third-party exclusion scheme; and a comprehensive main-floor smoking ban with approved smoking lounges has applied since 2019 [regime details from statute, not re-read this session]. Direct advertising of games of fortune is prohibited in Macau under the advertising law, which is why the concessionaires' marketing — concerts, NBA China Games, branded entertainment — is entirely non-gaming in form, and why mainland-facing promotion is routed through entertainment and MICE rather than casino product.

Data on problem-gambling prevalence, exclusion enrolments and AML filings for 2026 were not located in the regulator sources accessed this session (n/a). For an entrant the commercial implication is that customer acquisition in Macau is a venue-and-events business, not a performance-marketing business: there is no CRM-driven online funnel to buy, and the levers that work elsewhere (bonusing, affiliate marketing, app distribution) are either prohibited or legally hazardous when aimed at the ~95% Greater-China customer base.

segments.name: Non-casino betting & online
segments.headline: Sports betting is a sub-0.3%-of-GGR monopoly in regulatory limbo; racing is gone; online does not exist as a licensed product.
narrative: Outside the casino concessions, Macau's only material betting licence is Macau Slot Co. Ltd's exclusive concession for football and basketball betting, in place since 1998. DICJ's Q1-26 data show football wagering GGR of MOP90m (~$11.2m, -10% YoY) and basketball MOP73m (~$9.0m, +23.7%) — MOP163m (~$20.2m) combined, about 0.25% of Q1 casino GGR. The government extended the concession by one year to 5 June 2026 to allow a review of the future sports-betting model alongside lottery and non-gaming entertainment; the outcome of that review and the concession's status after 5 June 2026 could not be established from sources accessed this session (n/a). Q2 and Q3 sports-betting figures were not located (n/a), although trade coverage of Q3 referenced 'higher revenue' from these activities.

Racing has been wound up entirely: the Macao (Yat Yuen) Canidrome ended greyhound racing on 20 July 2018 and the Macau Horse Racing Company ended horse racing on 1 April 2024 (DICJ). Chinese lotteries (pacapio and similar instant/number games) remain licensed but are immaterial and no 2026 figures were located (n/a). The DICJ-regulated universe is therefore ~99.7% casino games of fortune.

Online gaming is simply absent from the legal framework: Law 16/2001 and its 2022 revision license 'casino games of fortune' in approved physical premises, there is no interactive or remote class, and no consultation on one has been launched. Combined with the 2022 illegal-gambling law and the mainland's cross-border gambling offences, the practical position is that online gaming is illegal both for operators in Macau and for the mainland customers they would target. Hengqin/Guangdong-Macao cooperation-zone initiatives have not included any gaming liberalisation.

For B2Tech, which presumably runs online sportsbook/casino elsewhere, the message is that Macau offers no addressable online market and no credible timeline for one; the sports-betting monopoly review is the only live licensing process, it is tiny, and nothing in the record suggests it will be opened to foreign online operators. The jurisdiction should be treated as a land-based B2B supply opportunity and as a demand barometer for Greater-China premium play, not as a market to enter.

highlights.text: Slots/ETGs are the only compounding product: 9M slot GGR ~MOP12.18bn (~$1.51bn, ~+19% YoY), share up to 6.8% of GGR from 5.5%, driven by capped table counts, satellite-floor reallocation and the deliberate migration of grind-mass play to machines — a structural B2B opening into a ~12,000-machine installed base now bought by just six counterparties.

Scale and fiscal alignment: Macau remains the world's largest casino market (FY25 GGR MOP247.4bn, ~$30.66bn, more than double the Las Vegas Strip) and the government's 84% revenue dependence means policy is oriented to protecting GGR — targets maintained, events subsidised, no tax rise contemplated.

Regulatory certainty to 2032: six concessions with fixed terms, a 35%+5% levy unchanged since 2002, consolidation finished (20 casinos, no satellites) — contract and counterparty risk for suppliers is low by emerging-market standards.

Top-of-funnel demand is still growing: 9M arrivals 32.18m (+8.5%), September +15.9%, Q3 11.2m; entertainment-led promotion (concerts, NBA China Games) is demonstrably pulling volume even if conversion to spend is weak.

VIP within concessionaire-run rooms is up ~10% over 9M (MOP52.4bn, ~$6.49bn) and recovered +6.3% QoQ in Q3, showing premium-direct capacity survived the junket purge — though Q1's +35% was hold- and base-assisted and October's reported -35% shows the volatility.

Non-gaming investment pledges and the 'international visitor' mandate create demand for entertainment, MICE and technology partners, with international arrivals (+3.4%) the KPI DICJ monitors — an adjacent services opening for non-gaming B2B.

lowlights.text: Demand has rolled over: five consecutive monthly YoY declines (Jun -12.1%, Jul -8.4%, Aug -1.2%, Sep -1.2%, Oct -10.0%), Q3 -3.8%, and an October fall in a Golden Week month — the World Cup excuse no longer covers it.

Premium-mass erosion is the core risk: mass baccarat -7.9% in Q3 (MOP33.61bn, ~$4.16bn), a MOP2.88bn (~$357m) decline exceeding the whole market's drop; GGR per visitor ~-15% in September as same-day visitors (+23.8%) displace overnight guests (+5.7%).

Closed market: no B2C entry before a re-tender ahead of 31 Dec 2032, no sub-concessions, no online licence class, a 2022 tender won entirely by incumbents on non-gaming pledges and local shareholding — an outside operator's probability of a licence is effectively nil this decade.

Levy economics: 40% effective tax on GGR plus annual premiums per table/machine and minimum-GGR-per-table top-ups [parameters unverified this session] leave operators with thin margins when GGR falls and wages rise (full-time gaming earnings +4.6% to MOP28,660, ~$3,551/month).

Policy risk is set in Beijing, not Macau: capital-control enforcement (Seaport's October VIP >-35%), cross-border gambling criminalisation and visa policy move GGR by double digits with no local recourse; ~94% of visitors are Greater China.

The government's 84% fiscal dependence makes it an aggressive principal: minimum-GGR rules, investment-pledge monitoring, national-security termination rights and the satellite ban show the state will restructure the industry when revenue is threatened.

Transparency gaps: DICJ does not publish operator shares; VIP is defined by table class not player type; quarterly and monthly series differ (~0.2%); one outlet misreported September GGR — any contract indexed to 'market GGR' needs a precise definition.

forecast.intro: The only official 'guidance' is the 2026 budget's GGR assumption of MOP236bn (~$29.24bn), set in late 2025 below the MOP247.4bn (~$30.66bn) actually earned in 2025 and left unchanged by CE Sam Hou Fai despite four (now five) months of YoY declines. With MOP208.79bn (~$25.87bn) banked through October, the target needs only MOP27.2bn (~$3.37bn) from November–December versus MOP41.98bn (~$5.20bn) a year earlier, so it will be met; the real question is the exit rate. Seaport models November at -6.1% YoY; carrying a similar decline into December yields FY2026 GGR of roughly MOP245–250bn (~$30.4–31.0bn), -1% to +1% YoY [estimate], and FY2026 gaming-tax receipts of MOP96–99bn (~$11.9–12.3bn) against a MOP92.53bn (~$11.47bn) budget [estimate]. The deterioration is concentrated in mass/premium-mass baccarat (Q3 -7.9%), partially offset by slots (+19%) and a flat-to-recovering VIP line; the 2027 budget assumption, due in the Legislative Assembly's November–December debate, is the next formal data point.

bridge.title: 2026 government GGR target

forecast.view: **Market:** we expect FY2026 to be Macau's first flat-to-down year since reopening and 2027 to deliver at best low-single-digit growth, with premium-mass GGR per visitor the binding constraint; slots should keep growing mid-teens and reach ~7–8% of GGR by end-2027 [estimate], while VIP oscillates within a 25–30% share band on hold and capital-control swings. **Rules:** no change to the 35%+5% levy, the six-concession cap or the online prohibition through 2032; direction of travel is incremental tightening (AML thresholds, promoter oversight, minimum-GGR enforcement, investment-pledge audits) plus pressure on concessionaires to deliver international visitation. The only live licensing decision is the Macau Slot sports-betting model, which is immaterial in revenue terms. **Fiscal:** receipts will beat budget again, keeping the government in surplus and removing any incentive to liberalise. **Swing factors:** PRC capital-control and visa policy (the dominant variable), mainland property/wealth effects on premium mass, a hold-driven VIP rebound, and whether Golden Week-style event programming can convert same-day volume into overnight spend. **For B2Tech:** treat Macau as a B2B machine/systems opportunity sized to a ~MOP16bn (~$2.0bn) annual slot win pool [estimate] and as a Greater-China demand barometer, not as an operating market.
